Capital One.

This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
U.S. stock markets took a real beating yesterday, turning in their worst performance since April
2025.
The tech-heavy NASDAQ index is officially in correction territory, down more than 10 percent
from its record high.
Investors are expressing fear that the AI boom is overblown and needs to be scaled back.
NPR's Windsor-Johnson reports voters all over the country have backed new limits on data
centers.
Voters in Maine backed a temporary pause on large data centers.
In Wisconsin, voters demanded a say over development at a former General Motor site.
One concern is who pays to power these projects.
Joshua Macy, a professor at Yale Law School, says Congress could change how those costs
are divided.
The big, big things that Congress could do are basically making data centers pay a significant
percentage of grid infrastructure costs.
But with President Trump pushing for faster development, Macy says it's unclear whether
the incoming Democratic majority can get the White House to agree to make developers pay
more for grid upgrades.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
A federal judge has blocked construction on President Trump's proposed triumphal arch
in Washington, D.C.
Emperors Rachel Treisman says the ruling came right after a panel had told the Trump administration
that it could proceed.
The National Capital Planning Commission, which is packed with Trump allies, voted to
approve the arch after an absolute marathon meeting.
It heard from some 130 people overwhelmingly against the arch, but after about nine hours,
the panel went ahead and gave it the green light.
The Trump administration had said it could start excavation work right after that.
But right around midnight, District Judge Tanya Chutkin stepped in and blocked construction
for 14 days.
That's a win for the plaintiffs suing over the arch, which started as a group including
Vietnam War veterans and now includes the governments of D.C. and Virginia.
NPR's Rachel Treisman prepared that report.
The Vatican says Pope Leo is on his way to South America for a nearly two-week trip.
Megan Williams reports from Rome.
The American-born Pope will visit Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru, meeting political leaders
celebrating mass before huge crowds and visiting survivors of clergy sexual abuse.
Leo became a Peruvian citizen and returns to a country struggling with corruption and
political instability.
Father John Lydon worked alongside him there for a decade.
The Pope is much more popular than the political leaders, so I think the political leaders
will be very careful not to create any conditions that spark of conflict.
Leo is expected to speak out on human rights, migrants, and the poor.
For NPR News, I'm Megan Williams in Rome.
You're listening to NPR.
The federal government will release its latest snapshots of the nation's employment picture
this morning.
Analysts suspect hiring may have been a bit stronger in October, perhaps, with some 60,000
new jobs created last month.
That would be better than September—about 29,000 new jobs were created at that time.
The weather is clearing on the border between southern Tennessee and northern Georgia.
Heavy flooding forced people to evacuate yesterday and submerged homes and businesses.
The National Weather Service says the rain over Blue Ridge, Georgia was a one-in-one-thousand-year
event.
More than 10 inches of rain fell in about six hours.
Those at Boston's Logan Airport have chosen a winner to voice announcements in the facility.
From member station WBUR, Andrea Perdomo Hernandez has more.
Forty-three-year-old Chris Denisi was among 6,000 people hoping to voice announcements
and information about airport services over the airport's PA system.
He was selected by public vote as the winner.
He says his mother encouraged him to apply.
Yeah, I thought maybe I had a shot, but when I heard how many people were auditioning,
I mean, no, I didn't think it was in my realm, but here I am today.
Denisi will start recording next week as the airport prepares for the start of the busy
holiday travel season.
Despite using his pipes for airport announcements, Denisi says he is keeping his day job as an
HVAC pipe fitter.
For NPR News, I'm Andrea Perdomo Hernandez in Boston.
And I'm Cora Vekulman, NPR News, from Washington.
